Subject: Post-call recap: Performance SLOs & concurrency needs

Hi Pablo —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap and next steps from our side: 

Summary of requirements we captured on the call:
- Latency target: p95 <= 200ms for text generation in the main user flow (60 token average).
- Streaming: client expects chunked streaming for tokens to render progress UI.
- Throughput: sustained 600 requests/minute at peak (spiky traffic during marketing campaigns).
- Concurrency: up to 150 concurrent active requests from the front-end (expected across ~75 active users), plus connection pooling from backend services.
- Burst capacity: short bursts up to ~300 concurrent requests for <2 minutes tolerated.

Open items for Redwood to confirm:
1) Confirm that hosted rate limits can accommodate sustained 600 rpm + bursts and the concurrency profile.
2) Clarify connection pooling semantics (we discussed whether a single connection = single concurrency slot).
3) Provide sample SLA language and a draft quota arrangement for Dedicated/Dedicated+Reserve.

Attachments: I’m including the matrix you mentioned (acme-performance-metrics.xlsx) and a draft SLA that we can iterate on (redwood-sla-draft.pdf).

Next steps:
- We (Marissa + Dev) will validate concurrency semantics and provide a recommended rate-limit configuration by EOD tomorrow.
- Pablo to share any absolute upper bounds (e.g., total monthly tokens or hard concurrent caps from your infra).
- Schedule a technical follow-up with your backend team if needed.

If anything in my recap is off, call it out — otherwise we’ll proceed with the items above.

Subject: Re: Post-call recap: Performance SLOs & concurrency needs

Thanks Marissa — looks accurate. Couple clarifications from our side:

- The p95 <=200ms is for the final rendered text generation call; upstream preprocessing can be slower. Good to call that out.
- Streaming is required — our UX team needs token-level chunks for progressive rendering.
- For concurrency: our front-end uses a connection pool in the backend; servers typically maintain 4 connections per instance and there are about 20 app instances in the initial rollout (so ~80 pooled connections). We expect number of instances to scale to 50 in a month.
- The 150 concurrent active requests estimate includes both pooled connections and short-lived worker calls (background requests). Assume worst-case concurrency = pooled connections * instances + 50 workers = 4 * 50 + 50 = 250.

Procurement: We’ll review the draft SLA and get back on standard terms. Also we need a line item for a guaranteed concurrency reservation or a mechanism to avoid 429s during campaign spikes.

Can you propose a quota/rate-limit configuration that supports sustained 600 rpm, streaming, and headroom for the 250 concurrent worst-case? Also need fallback behavior (queueing vs 429) and recommendation for Dedicated vs Hosted.

Best,
Pablo

Pablo — thanks for the details, that worst-case math is helpful. Proposed guidance below (high-level; tech follow-up recommended):

Redwood recommendation (hosted foundational plan -> Dedicated decision boundary):
- Sustained throughput: 600 rpm = 10 rps. With streaming enabled and 60-token averages, token throughput should be well within network/compute while respecting p95 target.
- Concurrency reservation: to avoid 429s during spikes, we recommend reserving 300 concurrency slots for your workload on Dedicated (covers your 250 worst-case plus 20% headroom).
- Hosted vs Dedicated: Hosted can handle the expected sustained 10 rps easily, but to guarantee concurrency reservation and strict latency SLOs during spikes (and to meet procurement/regulatory needs), Dedicated is recommended.

Rate-limit configuration options (pick one):
A) Hosted: soft rate limits — 600 rpm per tenant with burst window to 1200 rpm for 2 minutes; 200 concurrency soft cap with request queuing of up to 30s then 429. No hard reservation — possible throttling if overall cluster load is high.
B) Dedicated (recommended): hard concurrency reservation of 300 slots, sustained 600 rpm, short burst allowance to 1200 rpm for 2 minutes; queueing up to 60s before 429 (configurable). SLA addendum provides credits for breaches of latency or availability.

Connection pooling semantics: one active HTTP request occupying a server-side worker counts as a concurrency slot. Idle pooled connections do not consume a slot. For streaming/chunked responses, the slot is held for the life of the connection.

Fallback behavior: we recommend queueing + early 429s for synthetic overload protection (configurable thresholds). For customer UX, we typically implement exponential backoff client-side and graceful retry with jitter.

Next steps:
- Dev will validate exact resource footprint for 60-token average streaming and confirm token/sec expectations by tomorrow EOD.
- I’ll ask Ops to draft a Dedicated reservation quote (monthly commit) and SLA addendum for your procurement team.
- If you’re OK, we’ll schedule a 30-min tech sync to walk the backend team through pooling semantics and observe a simulated load.

Pablo — quick technical note from our infra side:

- Streaming: we hold the concurrency slot for the duration of the stream; if you expect long-running generations (>5s) this impacts slot duration. For 60-token averages we expect ~120-300ms per request on our optimized runtime on A100-class hosts (p95 in lab).
- Connection pooling: agreed — pooled idle sockets don’t consume slots; only active pushes/requests do.
- Suggested operational config for initial Dedicated deployment:
  * Concurrency reservation: 300 slots (as Marissa proposed).
  * Connection limit per client IP: 25 (to prevent accidental connection storms from misconfigured pools).
  * Burst policy: token-bucket style with refill for short bursts; allow 2x burst multiplier for 120s windows.

I’ll attach a short runbook to the tech sync and bring a simple load script we can run together. Let us know a couple of 30-min windows next week.

Thanks,
